layer.name: Business Layer
layer.description: Describes what the organization does independently of the software that supports it: business actors and roles, collaborations and interfaces, processes, functions, interactions and events, business services and business objects, and the business capabilities the organization has (ArchiMate 3.2 business layer, with the strategy layer's Capability). Elements here are realized by application services and consume no implementation detail. Modelling rules: actors fill roles, and roles and collaborations are assigned to the processes, functions and interactions they perform (assigned-to); behaviour is never assigned to an actor directly. Internal behaviour realizes business services, which interfaces offer (assigned-to) and which serve actors, roles and processes. Only behaviour accesses business objects and contracts; actors, roles and interfaces reach information through the behaviour assigned to them. Events trigger processes and interactions, and behaviour raises events (triggers); a hand-off between behaviours is flows-to, and a function, having no start, is reached by flows rather than triggered. A business capability is an ability the organization has: business functions and processes realize it, capabilities aggregate narrower capabilities, and software capabilities (product layer) contribute by realizing the business functions behind it. Business services and business capabilities carry the main link to motivation: services realize goals and outcomes, satisfy requirements and deliver value; capabilities support goals and realize outcomes; processes may also realize outcomes and satisfy requirements.

businessactor.title: BusinessActor
businessactor.description: An active structure element denoting a specific, nameable organizational entity (an individual person, a team or department, or an external organization such as a customer or supplier) that exists independently of any responsibility it holds and can be assigned to BusinessRoles to perform behavior. It denotes who the entity is, not what responsibility it carries. Use BusinessRole instead when the element names a set of responsibilities or authorizations, such as 'Approver' or 'Account Holder', that different people or organizations could fill, rather than a concrete entity. Use BusinessCollaboration instead when the element is a temporary or contextual grouping of roles that act jointly, such as a review board formed per case, rather than a standing organizational entity with its own identity. Use BusinessInterface instead when the element is a channel or access point, such as a call center, web portal or front desk, through which services are offered, rather than the entity offering or using them. Use BusinessObject instead when the code symbol is a data record about a party, such as a Customer table row, and the model needs the information itself rather than the organizational entity acting on it.

documentation.description: Free-text description of the organizational entity: who it is, whether it is internal or external, and its scope (person, unit or organization). Set it whenever the name alone does not make the entity's identity and boundary clear.

x-dr-evidence: A domain or party-model class or enum value naming an organizational entity, such as Customer, Supplier, Partner, Department or Organization, that holds identity fields (legal name, org ID, tax number) and is referenced as the initiator or owner of business transactions.

Requirements, use-case or BPMN documentation that lists named participants or pools (e.g., 'Actors: Customer, Finance Department, Payment Provider'), or a swimlane labeled with a department or external company.

Integration or tenant configuration that identifies concrete external organizations or internal units, such as partner IDs, tenant or organization records, or supplier onboarding entries, on whose behalf the system acts.

businesscapability.title: BusinessCapability
businesscapability.description: An ability the organization possesses or intends to possess, stated as what the business can do (e.g. 'Share data with partners', 'Settle insurance claims', 'Onboard new customers'), independent of how, by whom or with what software it is done. It is stable while the processes, functions, people and systems behind it change, and capabilities nest into a capability map. The business functions and processes that carry out the ability realize it, and software capabilities contribute through those business functions. Use SoftwareCapability (product layer) instead when the ability belongs to the software platform (e.g. 'Save documents to files'), which realizes a business function, rather than to the organization. Use BusinessFunction instead when the element is a standing area of work grouped by the competency or resources it needs (e.g. 'Claims Handling'), performed by a role, rather than the ability that such work realizes. Use BusinessService instead when the element is externally visible behaviour offered to a consumer, rather than an internal ability of the organization. Use Goal (motivation layer) instead when the element states an end the organization wants to reach rather than an ability it has.

documentation.description: Free-text description of the ability, its scope and the outcomes it enables; set whenever the name alone does not make the ability unambiguous.

level.description: Depth of the capability in the organization's capability map, 1 for a top-level capability.

businesscapability.x-dr-standard: ArchiMate 3.2 §7.3.1 Capability (Strategy Layer), placed in the business layer because DR has no strategy layer
x-dr-evidence: a business capability map, enterprise architecture document or strategy deck listing what the organization is able to do (e.g. a level-1/level-2 capability decomposition)
architecture decision records, roadmaps or OKRs that name an organizational ability to build or improve (e.g. 'become able to settle claims in one day') independent of any system
README or docs sections that map the software's modules to the business abilities they support

x-dr-distinguish.business.businessfunction: the element is a standing area of work performed by a role and grouped by competency, rather than the ability that work realizes
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessservice: the element is externally visible behaviour offered to a consumer rather than an internal ability
x-dr-distinguish.motivation.goal: the element states an end to reach rather than an ability the organization has

businesscollaboration.title: BusinessCollaboration
businesscollaboration.description: An active structure element that is a temporary or permanent grouping of two or more BusinessRoles (which BusinessActors fill) jointly assigned to collective behavior that none of them performs alone. It has no identity apart from its participants: removing participants below two dissolves it. Use BusinessRole instead when the element is a single set of responsibilities assignable to one actor, even if many actors may fill it. Use BusinessActor instead when the grouping is a standing organizational unit (department, team, partner company) with its own identity, independent of which roles it combines. Use BusinessInteraction instead when you are modelling the joint behavior itself (e.g. 'negotiate terms') rather than the group of participants that performs it. Use Contract instead when you are modelling the recorded agreement binding the parties rather than the parties acting together.

documentation.description: Free-text prose describing the collaboration's purpose, its participating roles and the collective behavior it exists to perform; set whenever the element name alone does not make the participants and scope clear.

x-dr-evidence: a BPMN collaboration diagram or workflow definition declaring two or more participant pools/lanes (e.g. Buyer and Seller) that exchange messages within one flow

a domain class or config entity such as ReviewBoard, Partnership or JointVenture whose fields reference multiple distinct participant role types and which is used to gate a multi-party step (e.g. requires approvals from each role)
approval or sign-off rules (e.g. a four-eyes or dual-control policy) listing several named roles that must act together before a business step completes

x-dr-distinguish.business.businessactor: the grouping is a standing organizational unit (department, team, partner company) with its own identity, independent of which roles it combines
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessinteraction: you are modelling the joint behavior itself (e.g. 'negotiate terms') rather than the group of participants that performs it
x-dr-distinguish.business.contract: you are modelling the recorded agreement binding the parties rather than the parties acting together

businessevent.title: BusinessEvent
businessevent.description: A behavior element that denotes an instantaneous, named occurrence of a business state change (e.g., order placed, contract signed, month-end reached) with no duration and no performer of its own. It exists only to trigger a BusinessProcess or BusinessInteraction, or to be raised by a BusinessProcess, BusinessFunction or BusinessInteraction; it is never accessed like information, and a hand-off between behaviours that involves no named occurrence is a flow, not an event. Use BusinessProcess instead when the element has duration, ordered steps, or a performing actor or role, rather than marking a single point in time. Use BusinessObject instead when the thing being modelled is the information record or message payload that carries the facts (e.g., the Order document), not the occurrence itself (OrderPlaced). Use BusinessInteraction instead when the element is collective behavior jointly carried out by several roles in a collaboration, not the moment that starts or ends that behavior.

documentation.description: Free-text explanation of the business occurrence, giving the state change it marks, its source, and the condition under which it is raised; set it whenever the event name alone does not make the trigger condition unambiguous.

type.description: Classification of the business event trigger

x-dr-evidence: Past-tense domain-event classes or records such as OrderPlaced or ContractSigned that are published to an event bus, outbox or message broker topic named after a business occurrence.
Cron or scheduler entries (e.g., a month-end or renewal-due job) whose firing starts a business workflow, indicating a timer-type event.
Start, intermediate or end events in BPMN or workflow-engine definitions, or business-named channels in an AsyncAPI or event-catalog document.

x-dr-distinguish.business.businessprocess: the element has duration, ordered steps, or a performing actor or role, rather than marking a single point in time.
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessobject: the thing being modelled is the information record or message payload that carries the facts (e.g., the Order document), not the occurrence itself (OrderPlaced).
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessinteraction: the element is collective behavior jointly carried out by several roles in a collaboration, not the moment that starts or ends that behavior.

businessfunction.title: BusinessFunction
businessfunction.description: A business behavior element that groups ongoing internal behavior by the competency, skill, knowledge or resource it requires (e.g. Accounting, Claims Handling, Procurement), performed by the BusinessRole assigned to it, with no defined start, end or ordered sequence of steps, so it is not triggered by an event; work reaches it through flows from processes and other functions. Use BusinessProcess instead when the behavior is an ordered sequence of steps with a trigger and a defined end result (e.g. 'Handle Insurance Claim from submission to payout') rather than a standing area of competence. Use BusinessService instead when the element describes externally visible behavior from the consumer's perspective (what is offered), rather than the internal grouping of work that realizes it. Use BusinessInteraction instead when the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more roles in a BusinessCollaboration rather than by a single role or actor. Use BusinessRole instead when the element names who holds responsibility (e.g. 'Claims Handler', 'Finance Department') rather than the behavior they perform (e.g. 'Claims Handling', 'Financial Accounting'). Use BusinessCapability instead when the element names an ability the organization has (e.g. 'Share data with partners'), independent of the competency area or roles whose work realizes it.

documentation.description: Free-text description of the competency area this function covers, its scope boundaries and the roles that perform it; set whenever the name alone does not make the grouped behavior unambiguous.

x-dr-evidence: top-level packages, modules or bounded contexts named after organizational competency areas (e.g. billing/, hr/, accounting/, procurement/) that own many related workflows rather than a single one

CODEOWNERS, team-ownership or service-catalog entries mapping a department or functional team to a group of modules, or permission scopes/menu sections grouped by functional area (e.g. 'finance:*', a 'Human Resources' navigation section)

architecture docs, capability or function maps, or ADRs listing functional areas of the business (e.g. a 'Business Functions' table or level-1 functional decomposition) referenced by code comments or module READMEs

x-dr-distinguish.business.businessprocess: the behavior is an ordered sequence of steps with a trigger and a defined end result (e.g. 'Handle Insurance Claim from submission to payout') rather than a standing area of competence.
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessservice: the element describes externally visible behavior from the consumer's perspective (what is offered), rather than the internal grouping of work that realizes it.
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessinteraction: the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more roles in a BusinessCollaboration rather than by a single role or actor.
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessrole: the element names who holds responsibility (e.g. 'Claims Handler', 'Finance Department') rather than the behavior they perform (e.g. 'Claims Handling', 'Financial Accounting').
x-dr-distinguish.business.businesscapability: the element names an ability the organization has, independent of the work and roles that realize it, rather than a standing area of work.

businessinteraction.title: BusinessInteraction
businessinteraction.description: A behavior element describing a unit of collective business behavior that two or more business roles carry out jointly within a BusinessCollaboration, such as negotiating terms or jointly approving a deal. It cannot be completed by any single participant acting alone. Use BusinessProcess instead when a single role or actor can carry the behavior through to its result, even if other parties are consulted or notified along the way. Use BusinessCollaboration instead when the element names the grouping of participating roles (who works together) rather than the joint behavior they perform (what they do together). Use BusinessFunction instead when the behavior is a stable, competency-based grouping (e.g., 'Partner Management') rather than a specific joint activity with a result. Use BusinessService instead when the element describes externally visible value offered to a consumer, with the joint internal behavior that delivers it hidden.

documentation.description: Free-text prose that names the participating roles, the joint result the interaction produces and its triggering events; set it whenever the participants or outcome are not obvious from the element name.

x-dr-evidence: A workflow, saga or state machine for one business transaction (e.g., Negotiation, JointApproval) whose transitions are guarded by different roles, and which reaches its terminal state only after actions from each party, such as buyer accepts and seller countersigns.
A BPMN collaboration or choreography diagram, or a use-case document listing two or more primary actors, that describes one shared activity spanning both parties' lanes.

API endpoints on a shared resource (e.g., /negotiations/{id}/offer and /negotiations/{id}/counter-offer) protected by distinct role authorizations, where completion requires calls from users holding each role.

x-dr-distinguish.business.businesscollaboration: the element names the grouping of participating roles (who works together) rather than the joint behavior they perform (what they do together)
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessfunction: the behavior is a stable, competency-based grouping (e.g., 'Partner Management') rather than a specific joint activity with a result

businessinterface.title: BusinessInterface
businessinterface.description: An active structure element representing a channel or point of access, such as a branch counter, call centre, customer portal or mailroom, through which a BusinessService is offered to and used by actors in the environment. It identifies where and how the service is reached, not the service itself or the person or role who staffs it. Use BusinessService instead when the element describes what value or behavior is offered to the consumer, independent of the channel through which it is reached. Use BusinessRole instead when the element is a set of responsibilities performed behind the access point, such as a call-centre agent, rather than the access point itself. Use Representation instead when the element is the perceptible form of information exchanged, such as an on-screen form or a printed letter, rather than the channel through which the service is accessed. Use BusinessActor instead when the element is the concrete organizational unit or person, such as a customer-service department, rather than the channel it operates.

documentation.description: Free-text description of the access channel, stating which BusinessServices it exposes, who uses it, and its medium (e.g. phone, web, in person); set it for every instance so the channel's scope is unambiguous.

x-dr-evidence: an enum or lookup table of customer contact channels (e.g. Channel { WEB, PHONE, BRANCH, EMAIL, PARTNER_PORTAL }) used to tag incoming requests or orders
channel-specific intake configuration, such as IVR or call-routing menus, a contact-centre queue definition, or a branch/portal entry module that routes customers to a named service
product or support documentation stating how customers reach a service (e.g. 'claims can be filed via the self-service portal, by phone, or at a branch')

x-dr-distinguish.business.businessrole: the element is a set of responsibilities performed behind the access point, such as a call-centre agent, rather than the access point itself
x-dr-distinguish.business.representation: the element is the perceptible form of information exchanged, such as an on-screen form or a printed letter, rather than the channel through which the service is accessed

businessobject.title: BusinessObject
businessobject.description: A passive structure element representing a business concept or unit of information (e.g., Order, Invoice, Claim, Customer record) that business behavior creates, reads, updates or deletes. It is identified by its business meaning and lifecycle, independent of storage format, schema or presentation. Use Contract instead when the information is specifically an agreement that sets out obligations, rights or terms between a provider and a consumer (e.g., SLA, policy terms, subscription agreement). Use Representation instead when the element is the perceptible form or media format in which the information is shown or exchanged (a PDF invoice, an HTML order form), not the information concept itself. Use BusinessEvent instead when the thing being modelled is a state change or occurrence (an order was placed) rather than the information entity that the occurrence concerns (the order). Use Product instead when the element is a bundle of services and contracts offered to customers as a value proposition, rather than a piece of information acted upon.

documentation.description: Free-text business definition of the object: what it means to the organization, its key information content and its lifecycle. Write it in domain vocabulary without storage or schema detail, and set it whenever the name alone is ambiguous.

x-dr-evidence: a domain-model class or aggregate root named with a business noun (Order, Invoice, Claim) in a domain/model package, referenced by several workflow or use-case handlers
a lifecycle status enum or state machine on that entity (e.g., DRAFT, SUBMITTED, APPROVED, CANCELLED) whose transitions are driven by business process steps
an entry in a business glossary, ubiquitous-language document or requirements spec that defines the term, with matching names in database tables, API schemas or JSON Schema titles

x-dr-distinguish.business.contract: the information is specifically an agreement that sets out obligations, rights or terms between a provider and a consumer (e.g., SLA, policy terms, subscription agreement)
x-dr-distinguish.business.representation: the element is the perceptible form or media format in which the information is shown or exchanged (a PDF invoice, an HTML order form), not the information concept itself
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessevent: the thing being modelled is a state change or occurrence (an order was placed) rather than the information entity that the occurrence concerns (the order)
x-dr-distinguish.business.product: the element is a bundle of services and contracts offered to customers as a value proposition, rather than a piece of information acted upon

businessprocess.title: BusinessProcess
businessprocess.description: A business behavior element, performed by the BusinessRole assigned to it (BusinessActors take part by filling that role), that consists of an ordered sequence of business activities with a defined start (a BusinessEvent or internal initiation) and a defined end state yielding a specific result, such as a delivered BusinessObject or a fulfilled request, for a customer or stakeholder. Use BusinessFunction instead when the behavior is a stable grouping of work by competency, skill or resource (e.g. 'Accounts Payable') with no inherent start trigger, step order or end result. Use BusinessInteraction instead when the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more roles acting as a BusinessCollaboration rather than by a single role or actor. Use BusinessService instead when you are describing the externally visible value offered to a consumer (what is provided), not the internal sequence of steps that delivers it (how it is done). Use BusinessEvent instead when the element is an instantaneous state change (e.g. 'Order Placed') that starts or ends a process, not the activity that runs between such changes.

documentation.description: Free-text prose describing the process's trigger, main steps, performing role, and end result, written in business terms; set whenever the name alone does not make the start and end conditions clear.

x-dr-evidence: A workflow or orchestration definition (BPMN file, Camunda/Temporal/Step Functions workflow, saga class) named after a business outcome, e.g. OrderFulfillmentWorkflow, whose steps run in a declared order.
A state machine or status enum on a business entity whose transitions follow a business lifecycle (e.g. SUBMITTED → APPROVED → SHIPPED) and are driven by a single orchestrating service method.
Documentation, runbooks or user stories that describe a numbered sequence of business steps from a trigger to a completion criterion, owned by a named role (e.g. 'claims handler').

x-dr-distinguish.business.businessfunction: the behavior is a stable grouping of work by competency, skill or resource (e.g. 'Accounts Payable') with no inherent start trigger, step order or end result.
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessinteraction: the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more roles acting as a BusinessCollaboration rather than by a single role or actor.
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessservice: you are describing the externally visible value offered to a consumer (what is provided), not the internal sequence of steps that delivers it (how it is done).
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessevent: the element is an instantaneous state change (e.g. 'Order Placed') that starts or ends a process, not the activity that runs between such changes.

businessrole.title: BusinessRole
businessrole.description: An active structure element naming a responsibility position in the organization (e.g., Claims Adjuster, Approver, Customer) that business behavior is assigned to and that one or more BusinessActors can fill. It is defined by what is expected of whoever occupies it, not by the identity of a particular person, department or organization. Use BusinessActor instead when the element is a specific, identifiable person, department, team or external organization, such as 'Finance Department' or 'Acme Ltd', rather than a position that different actors could fill. Use BusinessCollaboration instead when the element is a temporary or permanent grouping of two or more roles acting jointly, such as 'Buyer–Seller Negotiation', rather than a single responsibility position. Use BusinessFunction instead when the name denotes a capability-based grouping of behavior, such as 'Claims Handling', rather than the position responsible for performing it, such as 'Claims Handler'. Use BusinessInterface instead when the element is a channel or access point through which a service is offered, such as a call center, portal or front desk, rather than the responsibility held by whoever staffs it.

documentation.description: Free-text description of the role's responsibilities, required skills or authorizations, and typical occupying actors; set it whenever the role name alone does not make the scope of responsibility clear.

x-dr-evidence: An enum, constant set or lookup table of job-like user categories (e.g., APPROVER, UNDERWRITER, CASE_WORKER, CUSTOMER) that workflow or task-assignment logic uses to route work, rather than to name individual users.

Workflow or BPMN definitions that name a responsibility as a swimlane, candidateGroup or task assignee (e.g., camunda:candidateGroups="claims-adjuster"), or approval-chain configuration such as 'requires sign-off by Finance Approver'.
Requirements artifacts or user stories phrased 'As a <role>, I want…', or RACI and responsibility matrices listing positions against processes or tasks.

x-dr-distinguish.business.businesscollaboration: the element is a temporary or permanent grouping of two or more roles acting jointly, such as 'Buyer–Seller Negotiation', rather than a single responsibility position.
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessfunction: the name denotes a capability-based grouping of behavior, such as 'Claims Handling', rather than the position responsible for performing it, such as 'Claims Handler'.
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessinterface: the element is a channel or access point through which a service is offered, such as a call center, portal or front desk, rather than the responsibility held by whoever staffs it.

businessservice.title: BusinessService
businessservice.description: A behavior element that names an explicitly defined, externally visible unit of business behavior offered to customers or other stakeholders, such as 'Claims Handling' or 'Order Delivery'. It is described by the value and outcome the consumer receives, independent of the processes, functions, or software that realize it. Use BusinessProcess instead when the element describes the internal ordered steps, triggers, and hand-offs that produce a result, rather than the offering as the consumer sees it. Use BusinessFunction instead when the element is an internal grouping of behavior by competency or organizational capability, such as Finance or HR, that is not offered to a consumer as a named service. Use BusinessInterface instead when the element is the access point or channel through which the service is obtained, such as a call center, web portal, or branch counter, rather than the behavior itself. Use Product instead when the element is a marketed bundle of one or more services together with contracts or terms, sold or offered as a single package.

documentation.description: Free-text description of the service from the consumer's perspective: the need it fulfills, its intended consumers, and any service levels. Set it whenever the name alone does not make the offered outcome clear.

x-dr-evidence: A service catalog, SLA, or operating-level document entry that names a customer-facing offering (e.g. 'Claims Handling') with its consumers, availability hours, and service levels.
An OpenAPI tag, bounded-context module, or top-level domain package whose description states a business outcome for external consumers and groups several operations that support it.
A pricing page, terms-of-service text, or plan/entitlement configuration listing named services a customer is entitled to receive (e.g. 'Premium Support', 'Same-day Shipping').

x-dr-distinguish.business.businessfunction: the element is an internal grouping of behavior by competency or organizational capability, such as Finance or HR, that is not offered to a consumer as a named service.
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessinterface: the element is the access point or channel through which the service is obtained, such as a call center, web portal, or branch counter, rather than the behavior itself.
x-dr-distinguish.business.product: the element is a marketed bundle of one or more services together with contracts or terms, sold or offered as a single package.

contract.title: Contract
contract.description: A business object that records an agreement between two or more parties, typically a service provider and a consumer, stating the obligations, rights, and terms (e.g., SLA levels, pricing, durations, penalties) that govern how a business service or product is delivered and used. It is information acted upon, not behavior or an actor. Use BusinessObject instead when the information has business relevance but does not bind identified parties to obligations, rights, or terms (e.g., an invoice, order, or customer record). Use Representation instead when the element is the perceptible form of the agreement, such as the signed PDF, HTML terms page, or on-screen acceptance form, rather than the agreement's content. Use Product instead when the element is the offered bundle of services and contracts sold to a market, rather than the terms attached to it. Use BusinessEvent instead when the element is the state change of the agreement, such as a contract being signed, renewed, or terminated, rather than the agreement itself.

documentation.description: Free-text explanation of the agreement: the parties, the services or product it covers, and its key obligations and terms. Set it whenever the element name alone does not identify which agreement is meant.

x-dr-evidence: A domain class or schema named Agreement, Contract, Subscription, or ServiceLevelAgreement with fields such as parties, effectiveDate, expiryDate, termsVersion, and obligations or penalties
SLA or SLO configuration files that declare uptime, response-time, or support-tier commitments bound to a named customer plan or tier
Versioned terms-of-service, license, or data-processing-agreement documents in the repository, with code that records a user's acceptance of a specific terms version

x-dr-distinguish.business.representation: the element is the perceptible form of the agreement, such as the signed PDF, HTML terms page, or on-screen acceptance form, rather than the agreement's content
x-dr-distinguish.business.product: the element is the offered bundle of services and contracts sold to a market, rather than the terms attached to it
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessevent: the element is the state change of the agreement, such as a contract being signed, renewed, or terminated, rather than the agreement itself

product.title: Product
product.description: A composite element that bundles a named offering of one or more BusinessServices, optionally with application or technology services and business objects, together with the Contract that governs it, and that is offered as a whole to customers or markets. It is identified by what is sold or subscribed to, not by any single behavior or document within it. Use BusinessService instead when the element is a single externally visible unit of business behavior rather than a named, packaged offering combining several services with terms. Use Contract instead when the element is the agreement itself (terms, obligations, SLA, rights) rather than the offering those terms are attached to. Use BusinessObject instead when the element is information the business manipulates, such as a catalog entity or a 'Product' record or class in an e-commerce domain model describing goods for sale, rather than the offering bundle itself.

documentation.description: Free-text description of the offering: its name as marketed, target customers or market, included services, and governing terms. Set it whenever the element is created so reviewers can tell this bundle apart from others.

x-dr-evidence: A plan, tier or SKU definition (e.g. a PLANS constant, Stripe product/price IDs, a billing config listing 'Basic/Pro/Enterprise') that enumerates which capabilities or services each offering includes.
An entitlements or feature-gating map keyed by subscription plan or edition, deciding which services a customer may use based on what they purchased.
Pricing-page content, product sheets or onboarding docs that present a named offering together with links to its terms of service, SLA or license agreement.

x-dr-distinguish.business.businessservice: the element is a single externally visible unit of business behavior rather than a named, packaged offering combining several services with terms.
x-dr-distinguish.business.contract: the element is the agreement itself (terms, obligations, SLA, rights) rather than the offering those terms are attached to.
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessobject: the element is information the business manipulates, such as a catalog entity or a 'Product' record or class in an e-commerce domain model describing goods for sale, rather than the offering bundle itself.

representation.title: Representation
representation.description: A passive structure element that is a concrete, perceptible form (document layout, file format, printed or on-screen rendering) in which the information of a BusinessObject or Contract is conveyed to people. It captures how the information looks or is encoded, not what the information means. Use BusinessObject instead when the element is the business information concept itself (e.g., Invoice, Order) independent of any rendering or file format. Use Contract instead when the element is the agreement with its obligations and terms, rather than the signed PDF or printed form carrying it. Use BusinessInterface instead when the element is an access point (portal, counter, call centre) through which a service is offered, rather than the form of information delivered through it.

documentation.description: Free-text description of the representation, such as its audience, layout, channel (printed, emailed, on-screen), and which business object it carries. Set it whenever the name alone does not identify the rendering.

format.description: The media format of this representation

x-dr-evidence: a document or report template (e.g., Jasper/Thymeleaf/Handlebars/LaTeX template, .docx template) that renders a business entity such as an invoice or statement
a PDF/CSV/XML export generator, such as a class named InvoicePdfRenderer or StatementExporter, that produces a file with a fixed layout for end users
a printable or on-screen form definition (HTML form template, print stylesheet, email template) that presents a business document to customers or staff

x-dr-distinguish.business.businessobject: the element is the business information concept itself (e.g., Invoice, Order) independent of any rendering or file format.
x-dr-distinguish.business.contract: the element is the agreement with its obligations and terms, rather than the signed PDF or printed form carrying it.
x-dr-distinguish.business.businessinterface: the element is an access point (portal, counter, call centre) through which a service is offered, rather than the form of information delivered through it.

business.businessactor.assigned-to.busin.description: The actor fills the role and takes on its responsibilities; this is how a person, team or organization comes to perform business behaviour, since behaviour is assigned to roles rather than to actors directly.

business.businessactor.references.motiva.description: The actor acts on behalf of the stakeholder, so the stakeholder's concerns and drivers apply to what the actor does in the organization.

business.businesscapability.aggregates.b.description: The narrower capability is part of the wider one in the organization's capability map; it keeps its own identity and may be grouped under more than one parent.

business.businesscapability.realizes.mot.description: Exercising the capability produces the outcome, the end result the organization wants.

business.businesscapability.supports.mot.description: Having the capability helps the organization reach the goal, which is why the capability is worth building or keeping.

business.businesscollaboration.aggregate.description: The role is a participant in the collaboration; the role exists on its own and can take part in several collaborations, and the collaboration has no identity apart from the roles it groups.

business.businesscollaboration.assigned-.description: The collaboration carries out the interaction jointly; no single participating role can complete it alone.

business.businessevent.triggers.business.description: The occurrence of the event starts a run of the interaction among the collaboration's participants.
The occurrence of the event is the start trigger that launches a run of the process's ordered steps; use it for the event a process waits for, not for a hand-off between processes, which is flows-to.

business.businessfunction.accesses.busin.description: The function creates, reads, updates or deletes the business object while carrying out its ongoing behaviour.
The function reads or maintains the terms of the contract as part of its ongoing behaviour, for example when contract management records or renews agreements.

business.businessfunction.composes.busin.description: The narrower function is part of the wider one and exists only within it, so the function decomposes into the competencies that make it up.

business.businessfunction.flows-to.busin.description: Work or information produced by the upstream function passes to the downstream function, which continues with it.
Work or information produced by the function is handed to the process, which uses it in its ordered steps.

business.businessfunction.realizes.busin.description: The business function's standing work is what gives the organization the capability; as the work and the people doing it change, the capability stays.
The function's ongoing behaviour is what makes the service available to its consumers.

business.businessfunction.triggers.busin.description: The function raises the event when it reaches a business state change worth naming, such as a monthly close being completed.

business.businessinteraction.accesses.bu.description: The interaction's participants jointly create, read, update or delete the business object, as when a negotiation produces agreed terms.

business.businessinteraction.flows-to.bu.description: The result of the upstream interaction passes to the downstream interaction, which continues the joint work.
The result of the interaction is handed to the process, which carries it forward with a single performing role.

business.businessinteraction.realizes.bu.description: The interaction's joint behaviour is what makes the service available, so the service exists only because the participants work together.

business.businessinteraction.triggers.bu.description: The interaction raises the event when its joint behaviour reaches a named state change, such as a deal being agreed.

business.businessinterface.assigned-to.b.description: The interface is the channel through which the service is offered, so the service is reached at that point of access, such as a portal, counter or call centre.

business.businessinterface.serves.busine.description: The actor uses the interface as its point of access to the organization's services.
Whoever fills the role uses the interface as its point of access to the organization's services.

business.businessobject.composes.busines.description: The part object exists only within the whole object, as order lines exist only within an order.

business.businessobject.references.appli.description: The data object records the business object's information in an application, so the business concept can be traced to the data that holds it.

business.businessprocess.accesses.busine.description: One or more steps of the process create, read, update or delete the business object.
One or more steps of the process read or change the contract, for example checking an entitlement or recording a signature.

business.businessprocess.constrained-by..description: The separation-of-duty rule limits which roles may perform the process's steps, so that no one role carries a sensitive sequence end to end.

business.businessprocess.flows-to.busine.description: Work or information produced by the process is handed to the function, which continues with it as part of its ongoing behaviour.

When the upstream process completes or reaches a hand-off point, its work or result passes to the downstream process, which continues the end-to-end sequence; use it for the sequence between processes, and triggers only for an event.

business.businessprocess.realizes.busine.description: Running the business process is how the organization exercises the capability, so the process is one concrete means by which the capability exists.
The process's ordered steps are what makes the service available to its consumers.

business.businessprocess.realizes.motiva.description: Completing the process produces the outcome, the end result the organization wants.

business.businessprocess.satisfies.motiv.description: The process is how the organization meets the requirement.

business.businessprocess.triggers.busine.description: The process raises the event, typically when it ends or passes a milestone, such as an order being shipped.

business.businessrole.assigned-to.busine.description: Whoever fills the role carries out the function's ongoing behaviour.
The role is one of the participants that carry out the interaction jointly.
Whoever fills the role performs the process and is responsible for its result.

business.businessrole.composes.business..description: The narrower role is part of the wider one and exists only within it, so the wider role's responsibilities include the narrower role's.

business.businessrole.references.motivat.description: The role acts on behalf of the stakeholder, so the stakeholder's concerns and drivers apply to whoever fills the role.

business.businessservice.accesses.busine.description: Delivering the service reads the contract's terms, for example checking a consumer's entitlement or service level.

business.businessservice.delivers.busine.description: The service hands the business object to its consumer as its result, as a policy issuance service delivers a policy.

business.businessservice.delivers.motiva.description: Consumers of the service gain the value; the value is why the service is offered.

business.businessservice.realizes.motiva.description: Offering the service achieves the goal; this is the business layer's main link to the organization's goals.
Offering the service produces the outcome its consumers or the organization want.

business.businessservice.satisfies.motiv.description: The service is how the organization meets the requirement.

business.businessservice.serves.business.description: The actor uses the service; the actor is a consumer, such as a customer or supplier, of what the service offers.
One or more steps of the process use the service to get the result the sequence needs.
Whoever fills the role uses the service as a consumer of what it offers.

business.contract.governs.business.busin.description: The contract sets the obligations, rights and terms, such as service levels, prices and penalties, under which the service is delivered and used.

business.product.aggregates.business.bus.description: The service is one of the offerings bundled into the product; it exists on its own and can be part of several products.

business.product.composes.business.contr.description: The contract states the terms of the product and exists only as part of it.

business.representation.realizes.busines.description: The representation is a perceptible form of the business object, such as a printed invoice or an on-screen statement.
The representation is a perceptible form of the contract, such as the signed document or its PDF.
